item.title: Can't Beat Free: Gemma 4 31B on AMD Token Lab, with a Local Chat Page and an ADK Agent
item.dc:creator: xbill
item.content:encoded:
This article provides a step by step guide to calling Gemma 4 31B on AMD GPUs through AMD Token Lab, a free API that comes with membership of the AMD AI Developer Program. A local chat page, a terminal client and a small ADK agent are built on top of it, all from the same rig.

https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/tree/main/tokenlab-sglang-amd-31b

The question is simple: what can you build on an API that costs nothing? Token Lab gives every program member a key, a 30-day access period and a points budget, with no credit card and no credit request. Every figure below comes from requests sent to it on 2026–11–13.

What Is AMD Token Lab?

Token Lab describes itself as an OpenAI-compatible API “for leading open models, served on AMD Instinct and Radeon”. The base URL is https://api.tokenlab.amd.com/v1, and it works from curl, the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, LangChain, and AMD AI Notebooks.

It is one of the member perks of the AMD AI Developer Program. The program’s Cloud Credits page offers three options: AMD Instinct Developer Cloud, Fireworks AI, and Token Lab. Token Lab is the only one marked “No credit request needed”.

The catalog held 10 models, every one marked Free: Gemma 4 31B, DeepSeek V4 Flash and V4.1 Flash, Qwen3.8 27B, three MiniCPM models, and three decision models. Gemma-4–31B-IT reads text and images and has a 262,144-token context.

What a new key came with:

Token Lab says points measure relative usage per model, with larger models using more points per token. Running everything in this article, 23 requests used 0.000335 of the 10 points.

At This Point You Should Have…

  • An email address for an AMD account
  • Python 3 with pip
  • For the agent: google-adk and litellm (pip install google-adk litellm)
  • A clone of gemma4-dev, or just the tokenlab-sglang-amd-31b directory

Step 1 — Join the AMD AI Developer Program

The program’s home page says it plainly: “The program is free to join and helps you build, optimize, and scale AI on AMD hardware.”

Go to https://developer.amd.com and choose Join the Program. New to AMD, the steps the page lists are:

  1. Complete the AMD AI Developer Program sign-up form
  2. Verify your email address
  3. Access AI Academy

With an existing AMD account, log in and open the join form instead.

Membership also lists a one-month DeepLearning.AI membership, early event registration, a private Discord with AMD engineers, and a monthly sweepstakes for a Radeon GPU or a Ryzen AI PC.

Step 2 — Get a Token Lab Key

Open https://notebooks.amd.com/tokenlab and sign in with AMD AI Developer Program (Global) Login. The page has three steps: get your key, copy the base URL, call a model from the catalog.

The dashboard shows points remaining, requests in the last 30 days, days left, the rate limit and the key’s status, with buttons to regenerate or revoke the key. Regenerating keeps your points and your access period.

Put the key in the rig’s .env, readable only by you and never committed:

cd tokenlab-sglang-amd-31b
umask 077; echo 'TOKENLAB_API_KEY=tl-...' > .env

The base URL and the model name live in the committed tpu.env:

TOKENLAB_BASE_URL=https://api.tokenlab.amd.com/v1
MODEL_NAME=Gemma-4-31B-IT

Step 3 — The First Call

make query sends one chat completion and prints the raw reply:

$ make query
{
  "model": "Gemma-4-31B-IT",
  "choices": [
    {
      "message": {
        "role": "assistant",
        "content": "The capital of Australia is Canberra."
      },
      "finish_reason": "stop",
      "matched_stop": 106
    }
  ],
  "usage": {
    "prompt_tokens": 20,
    "completion_tokens": 8,
    "cost": 1.1228e-06
  }
}

Every reply carries a cost field in points, so a client can keep its own running total.

Step 4 — What Is Behind the Endpoint

make models prints the model card Token Lab publishes:

{
  "id": "Gemma-4-31B-IT",
  "name": "Gemma 4 31B",
  "description": "Dynamic sglang-router service managed by Model Ops",
  "context_length": 262144,
  "supported_parameters": ["temperature", "max_tokens", "top_p", "stream",
    "response_format", "tools", "tool_choice", "reasoning_effort"],
  "architecture": {"input_modalities": ["text", "image"], "output_modalities": ["text"]}
}

Gemma 4 31B runs on SGLang: the card says “sglang-router”, and replies carry SGLang’s matched_stop field. Three MiniCPM models in the same catalog are "vllm-router" services. Token Lab names the hardware only as AMD Instinct and Radeon.

Tool calling and JSON output are both in the supported parameters, which is what the agent in Step 7 needs.

Step 5 — A Local Chat Page

chat_ui.py is the chat page from this repo's TPU v5e vLLM rig, pointed at Token Lab. It is standard-library Python: it serves one page on 127.0.0.1 and forwards /v1/* to Token Lab with the key attached, so the key stays on your machine and never reaches the browser.

$ make ui
Chat UI on http://localhost:8766 -> https://api.tokenlab.amd.com/v1 (Gemma-4-31B-IT)

The side panel has max tokens, temperature, top-p, a thinking switch and a system prompt; the last reply’s first-token time, decode rate, tokens and points; the model card; and the session’s totals. That reply took 4.96 s to its first token, decoded at 9.5 tokens per second, and used 0.00000942 points.

The 🖼 button attaches an image, sent as a data URL in the OpenAI image format. Thinking turns on Gemma’s reasoning with chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking, and the reasoning streams into a collapsible section above the answer.

Step 6 — From the Terminal

ask.py follows the ask clients of this repo's GTX 1650 Ti rigs: one question and exit, a pipe, or a conversation with memory.

$ make bin        # links ~/bin/ask-tokenlab
$ echo "Canberra is the capital of Australia." | ask-tokenlab translate to French
**Canberra est la capitale de l'Australie.**

Piped input becomes the material and the arguments become the instruction. -T turns thinking on, -I photo.jpg attaches an image, -r prints the raw JSON, and no arguments opens a conversation where ! clears the history.

Step 7 — A Sample ADK Agent

tokenlab_agent/ is a small agent for Google's Agent Development Kit. ADK reaches Token Lab through LiteLLM's OpenAI provider, so the whole connection is one model object:

model = LiteLlm(
    model="openai/Gemma-4-31B-IT",
    api_base="https://api.tokenlab.amd.com/v1",
    api_key=TOKENLAB_API_KEY,
    num_retries=30,
    timeout=600,
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}},
)

The agent has two tools. list_tokenlab_models returns what Token Lab serves right now. count_and_range counts, filters and finds the minimum and maximum in code, so the model quotes an exact figure and states the filter it used:

def count_and_range(numbers: list[float], at_least: Optional[float] = None,
                    below: Optional[float] = None) -> dict:
    """Count the numbers that satisfy at_least <= x < below, and give their min, max and sum."""

run_agent.py runs one turn and prints every tool call with its time:

$ python3 run_agent.py
   8.1s call   count_and_range({"at_least": 10, "numbers": [0, 2, 3, 20, 21, 22, 23, 10, 11, 12, 13]})
   8.1s result {"filter": "10 <= x", "total_values": 11, "count": 8, "min": 10, "max": 23, "sum": 132}
  12.3s answer There are 8 values that are 10 or more, using the filter "10 <= x".

Gemma read “10 or more” as at_least: 10, the tool returned 8, and the answer quoted the tool's count and filter. The second tool:

$ python3 run_agent.py "Which models on Token Lab are served by vLLM, and which by SGLang? Short list."
  25.7s call   list_tokenlab_models({})
  38.4s result {"models": [{"id": "Clef", "service": "Dynamic aux-router service managed by Model Ops", ...
  48.9s answer **vLLM:**
* MiniCPM5-2B
* MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B
* MiniCPM-V-4.7-35B-A3B
**SGLang:**
* DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
* DeepSeek-V4-Flash
* Gemma-4-31B-IT
* Qwen3.8-27B

The same agent runs in ADK’s own tools: make agent for adk run in the terminal and make agent-web for adk web on port 8767.

Step 8 — How Fast Is Free?

One streamed request at a time, temperature 0, from a laptop:

Decode speed ranged from 2.0 to 9.5 tokens per second over the day for one request, and the first token arrived after 1.2 to 5.0 s. In the timed runs the reply headers arrived within half a second, and the stream carried keep-alive pings until the first token.

The endpoint is shared by every Token Lab user. Gemma 4 31B has a limit of 128 requests at once across all of them, and a request over it gets HTTP 429 with Retry-After: 1. These numbers describe Token Lab's load on the day, and say nothing about the speed of the GPUs behind it.

🔎 Tip: Retry Before the Stream Starts

Token Lab answers 429 when the model is at its shared limit or your key is over 20 requests a minute, and 502, 503 or 504 when a backend restarts. Its FAQ asks clients to wait a few seconds and send the request again, honouring Retry-After.

tokenlab.py does that for the chat page and the terminal client, before the reply starts, and the agent gets it from LiteLLM's num_retries. A stream that breaks after it started has no status code to retry on: a complete stream ends with data: [DONE], and the chat page flags a reply that ends without it.

The stream also carries lines a strict parser trips on: : ping while queued, id: N after each event, and event: done before [DONE]. Read only the data: lines.

Compare and Contrast

The three options on the program’s Cloud Credits page:

So, Which One?

Start with Token Lab. It costs nothing and needs no request and no setup beyond a key. It is the place to try Gemma 4 31B against the other models in the catalog, to build a prototype, and to wire up an agent.

When a prototype needs speed you can rely on, a model outside the catalog, or a server of its own, request the AMD Instinct Developer Cloud credit and serve the model yourself; this repo’s gpu-vllm-mi300x-31b rig serves the same model on vLLM.

Summary

The goal of this article was to find what can be built on AMD Token Lab, the free API that comes with the AMD AI Developer Program. The key to the solution was one small client module that holds the key, retries what Token Lab asks to be retried, and serves a chat page, a terminal client and an ADK agent. The results were:

  • 🟢 Joining the program is free, and Token Lab needs no credit request: a key comes with 10 points, 30 days and 20 requests per minute.
  • 🟢 Gemma 4 31B answers text and images, with thinking, tools and a 262,144-token context, on the OpenAI API.
  • 🟢 Everything in this article used 0.000335 of the 10 points over 23 requests.
  • 🟢 The local chat page keeps the key on your machine and shows each reply’s timings and points.
  • 🟢 An ADK agent reaches Token Lab with one LiteLlm object and calls tools: it answered a counting question from a tool's exact result.
  • ⚠️ The endpoint is shared: one request decoded at 2.0 to 9.5 tokens per second, and the first token took up to 5 s.
  • ⚠️ Gemma 4 31B runs on SGLang behind Token Lab, and the GPU model is not published.
  • ❌ A request over the shared 128-request limit gets 429 and must be sent again; a stream cut off mid-reply cannot be retried automatically.

Scope: one laptop calling api.tokenlab.amd.com on 2026-11-13, one request at a time, Gemma-4-31B-IT, temperature 0 for the timing table. Times include the network and other users' load on a shared service, so they change hour to hour. Concurrency, long prompts and answer accuracy were not measured. The agent used google-adk 2.13.0 and litellm 1.106.4.

The strategy for building on AMD Token Lab was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

References

  • tokenlab-sglang-amd-31b on GitHub
  • Evidence for this article
  • AMD AI Developer Program
  • AMD Token Lab
  • Google Agent Development Kit
  • LiteLLM
  • SGLang
  • Gemma 4 31B on Hugging Face
  • gemma4-dev on GitHub

Hope you enjoyed it!

item.title: Six Serving Engines on Four Accelerators: Gemma 4 E2B on an RTX 3050, a T4, an L4 and a TPU v5e
item.dc:creator: xbill
item.content:encoded:
This article provides a step by step comparison of the same inference serving engines on four accelerators: an 8 GB RTX 3050 in a desktop, a Tesla T4 on Compute Engine, an NVIDIA L4 in an EC2 G6, and one Cloud TPU v5e chip. Each one served Gemma 4 E2B on Google’s QAT 4-bit weights, and each has its own article; this one puts the four side by side.

https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev

The question is whether the engine to run changes with the chip. Each platform got the same prompts, the same 1-to-64-request load sweep and the same 1,319 GSM8K and 400 BFCL questions, with Google’s E2B drafter wherever the engine supports one. Every cross-platform figure below is read from the four ladders’ own result files and computed by rollup.py.

The Results in Brief

Answers do not depend on the chip. Five CUDA engines on three GPUs give 15 GSM8K scores between 0.8954 and 0.9030 and BFCL scores between 0.9150 and 0.9250, a spread of 4 questions. On the TPU the int4 builds score 0.8969 to 0.9007 and the bf16 engines 0.9113 to 0.9143. LiteRT-LM on Google’s int2/4/8 file is the lowest on every GPU.

For one request without a drafter, the chip sets the speed and the engines move together: on each GPU the five CUDA engines are within 1.07 to 1.16x of each other. The drafter separates them, and vLLM gains the most on every GPU: 1.90x on the 3050, 1.78x on the T4, 1.96x on the L4. vLLM with its drafter is the fastest engine for one request on all three GPUs. On the TPU the drafter does not fit beside vLLM, and SGLang-JAX is fastest at 159.9 tokens per second.

At 64 requests vLLM leads on the T4 and the L4 at both shapes, and its drafter still pays there. On the 3050 SGLang leads vLLM by 3% on long replies and vLLM leads on long prompts. On the TPU, SGLang-JAX with an E2B patch reaches 2.52x vLLM on long replies.

What Changes and What Stays

The same on every platform: Gemma 4 E2B, greedy decoding, thinking off for speed and accuracy, one engine at a time on the chip, and one Python interpreter with no virtual environment. On the three GPUs every engine version and checkpoint revision is the same: llama.cpp 7182ef71e, vLLM 0.33.0, SGLang 0.5.23, mistral.rs v0.9.5, LiteRT-LM 0.19.0, and the exact Q4_0 GGUF or the W4A16 checkpoint carrying the same 4-bit values. The TPU runs vLLM from its pinned TPU image on the same W4A16 checkpoint, and the JAX engines and SGLang-JAX on bf16 google/gemma-4-E2B-it.

llama.cpp and mistral.rs have no TPU backend.

At This Point You Should Have…

  • The four ladder articles, one per platform (References)
  • A clone: git clone https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev
  • docs/serving-engines-rollup/rollup.py, which reads each ladder's result files from evidence/ and prints every table below

Step 1 — One Method on Four Platforms

Each ladder ran the same three jobs per engine against one server start:

  • One request: six chat prompts of 256 tokens, three repeats, the geometric mean of each prompt’s median, end to end.
  • Load: sweep.py at 1 to 64 requests, two shapes (512 tokens in / 128 out and 128 in / 512 out), five repeats, a unique prompt per request so no prefix cache can hit.
  • Accuracy: gen_eval.py with all 1,319 GSM8K test questions and the 400 BFCL simple function-calling questions, one request at a time.
cd docs/serving-engines-rollup && python3 rollup.py
ONE REQUEST, tok/s end to end (six prompts, 256 tokens, geometric mean of medians)
engine                            3050                    T4                    L4                 v5e-1
vLLM                 121.1 / 230.5 (4)     108.4 / 193.0 (3)     140.4 / 275.3 (4)                 143.9

Each engine got the memory settings its chip allows, so the setting differs where the card does: mistral.rs holds 4 requests on the 3050 and T4 rigs and 32 on the L4.

Step 2 — Answer Quality on Every Chip

GSM8K / BFCL, one request at a time, no drafter:

The 15 CUDA GSM8K scores span 0.0076, and each ladder found its engines level with each other question by question. The drafters change no score on any GPU.

On the TPU:

The int4 builds score with the GPUs. The bf16 engines run about one point higher, and in the v5e ladder only SGLang-JAX’s lead over vLLM had a paired range above zero. vLLM is the only TPU engine that returns tool calls (BFCL 0.9200).

🔎 Tip: LiteRT-LM’s own file costs answers. Google’s gemma-4-E2B-it.litertlm mixes int2, int4 and int8 weights, and it scores 0.0046 to 0.0220 below the lowest CUDA engine on the same card. LiteRT-LM serving the exact Q4_0 build scores 0.8999 on the L4, level with the others.

Step 3 — One Request Without a Drafter

Tokens per second, end to end:

On each GPU the five CUDA engines sit close together: fastest over slowest is 1.113 on the 3050, 1.161 on the T4 and 1.073 on the L4. The chip moves them all at once. Against the L4, the same engine runs at 0.80 to 0.88x on the 3050 and 0.72 to 0.82x on the T4. vLLM on one v5e chip runs at 1.025x vLLM on the L4.

LiteRT-LM runs at 0.426 to 0.725x llama.cpp on the same card.

Step 4 — The Drafter for One Request

Best drafter against no drafter, same engine and card:

So the fastest engine for one request is vLLM with its drafter on every GPU: 230.5 tokens per second on the 3050, 193.0 on the T4 and 275.3 on the L4. Every gain is smallest on the T4, the oldest card. On the TPU vLLM with Google’s drafter runs out of memory during warmup:

Error allocating device buffer: Attempting to allocate 512.00M. That was not possible. There are 450.17M free.; (0x0x0_HBM0)

🔎 Tip: mistral.rs’s drafter fails on a T4. The T4 runs the target model in float16 and the drafter loads as bf16, and every drafted request fails with dtype mismatch in matmul, lhs: F16, rhs: BF16. On the 3050 and L4 it runs and is slower than no drafter.

Step 5–64 Requests at Once

Aggregate output tokens per second at 64 requests, each engine at its best setting, 128 in / 512 out:

512 in / 128 out:

vLLM leads on the T4 and the L4 at both shapes, by 1.283x and 1.522x over SGLang on long replies. On the 3050 SGLang leads vLLM by 1.032x on long replies and vLLM leads on long prompts. On the TPU SGLang-JAX leads vLLM by 2.516x on long replies and 2.141x on long prompts, with the bf16 model against vLLM’s int4 build, so engine and weights differ together there. PyTorch, LiteRT-LM, the JAX engine and the Rust model serve one request at a time.

Step 6 — The Drafter Under Load

vLLM’s best drafted setting against no drafter, at 64 requests:

On every card the best draft length falls as requests rise, from 3 or 4 tokens for one request to 1 token or none at 64, except the L4 on long replies, where 4 tokens stay best. The drafter still pays at 64 requests on the T4 and the L4, and on the 3050 it is level from 32. Each ladder found SGLang’s drafter losing under load: 0.30 to 0.49x of running without it at 64 on the 3050 and 0.69 to 0.73x on the L4.

Step 7 — The Same Engine on Another Chip

vLLM without a drafter, against vLLM on the L4:

One request depends little on the card; many requests depend a lot. vLLM’s output at 64 requests is 26.77x its one-request rate on the L4, 13.76x on the 3050, 11.69x on the v5e chip and 8.59x on the T4 (128 in / 512 out). So the v5e chip matches an L4 for one user and falls to 0.455x at 64 long replies.

Step 8 — What Each Platform Asks of Each Engine

SGLang needs patches on every platform for this checkpoint. On the T4 its own 4-bit kernels are built only for sm_80 and newer, and the patch sends them to vLLM’s Turing build.

Compare and Contrast

So, Which One?

On any of the three GPUs, run vLLM with Google’s W4A16 drafter. It is the fastest engine for one request on all three, and at 64 requests it leads on the T4 and the L4 and is within 3% of SGLang on the 3050; drop the draft length toward 1 token as load rises. llama.cpp with its drafter is the engine that runs as installed everywhere, and the right one for one user in under 3 GB. On one TPU v5e chip, vLLM from its pinned image is the engine that serves E2B with tool calls as shipped; SGLang-JAX with the E2B patch is 2.14 to 2.52x faster at 64 requests. The chip takes vLLM at 64 long replies from 871.8 tokens per second on the T4 to 3,715.7 on the L4, and leaves the answers where they were.

Summary

The goal of this article was to find whether the serving engine to run for Gemma 4 E2B changes with the accelerator. The key was running the same model, prompts, load sweep and question sets through the same engines on four chips, and computing every comparison from the ladders’ own result files. The results were:

  • 🟢 Five CUDA engines on three GPUs give 15 GSM8K scores between 0.8954 and 0.9030 and BFCL between 0.9150 and 0.9250; drafters change no score.
  • 🟢 vLLM with its drafter is the fastest engine for one request on every GPU: 230.5, 193.0 and 275.3 tokens per second on the 3050, T4 and L4.
  • 🟢 vLLM leads at 64 requests on the T4 and L4 at both shapes, and its drafter still pays there (1.34x and 1.22x on long replies).
  • 🟢 On one TPU v5e chip SGLang-JAX with an E2B patch is the fastest engine, 2.52x vLLM at 64 long replies.
  • ⚠️ For one request without a drafter the engines on each GPU are within 1.07 to 1.16x of each other; the chip sets the speed.
  • ⚠️ The drafter’s gain depends on the engine and the card: 1.78 to 1.96x for vLLM, 0.72 to 1.39x for SGLang, smallest on the T4.
  • ❌ vLLM with Google’s drafter runs out of memory on one v5e chip, and mistral.rs’s drafter fails on a T4.
  • ❌ SGLang needs patches for this checkpoint on all four platforms, and LiteRT-LM’s own int2/4/8 file scores lowest on every GPU.

Scope: one RTX 3050 OEM in a desktop, one Tesla T4 on a GCE n1-standard-2, one NVIDIA L4 on an EC2 g6.4xlarge and one flex-start TPU v5e chip, Gemma 4 E2B, greedy decoding, one engine at a time. The ladders ran on different days between 2026-10-14 and 2026-11-11, and the TPU ran different engines and bf16 weights for SGLang-JAX and the JAX engines, so the TPU rows compare engine and weights together. One-request speed is six prompts of 256 tokens, three repeats; load is two synthetic shapes at 1 to 64 requests, five repeats each; accuracy is one pass of GSM8K (1,319) and BFCL simple (400). Cost and power were not compared.

The strategy for comparing inference serving engines across GPUs and TPUs was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

References

  • Six Serving Engines, One 8 GB GPU: Gemma 4 E2B on an RTX 3050
  • Six Serving Engines on One Tesla T4: Gemma 4 E2B on a Turing GPU
  • Six Serving Engines on One EC2 G6: Gemma 4 E2B on an NVIDIA L4
  • Six Serving Engines on One Cloud TPU v5e Chip: Gemma 4 E2B
  • Porting Gemma 4 E2B to SGLang-JAX on One Cloud TPU v5e

  • SGLang

item.title: What Changes With the A2UI 1.0 Release
item.dc:creator: xbill
item.content:encoded:
This article walks through what changed between A2UI 0.9 and A2UI 1.0, how generated UI works on 1.0, and why it is better, using one currency agent built on both versions. A Google ADK agent on Gemini looks up exchange rates and answers with A2UI cards and charts, rendered by a Next.js CopilotKit front end over AG-UI.

https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1

On 0.9 the model wrote the UI as JSON, figures included. On 1.0 it writes one line and the server does the rest. A rate card for “Convert 100 USD to EUR” is 223 tokens of 0.9 JSON, 139 tokens of 1.0 Express, and 21 tokens as a 1.0 server-side macro call. A 90-day history chart is 1,060 tokens of 0.9 JSON and 21 as a macro call. Counted with the Gemini tokenizer, for the same components.

What Is A2UI?

A2UI is a protocol for agents that answer with UI. The agent sends a description of components (cards, text, buttons, charts) from a catalog the client implements, and the client renders them with its own native widgets. The agent never sends code, so the client decides what can run.

The Agent Used for the Comparison

The 0.9 build is commit d181ddb of the same repository. Everything after it is 1.0. Versions, read from the machine on 2026-11-11:

What Changed at a Glance

Read from the installed a2ui-core 0.6.0, which ships the 0.9 and 1.0 schemas side by side:

The last two rows belong to the agent SDK, a2ui-agent-sdk 0.11.0, which ships with the 1.0 protocol. The sections below take the changes one at a time: what 0.9 did, what 1.0 does, and what it buys.

Change 1 — A Whole Surface in One Message

On 0.9 a new surface took three messages: createSurface named the catalog, updateComponents sent the components, and updateDataModel filled in the data. The renderer held an empty surface until the last one arrived.

On 1.0 createSurface carries components and dataModel inline. This Express block, a form with a bound text field, a check and a button, compiles to both versions with the SDK's own compiler:

surface("main")
$/user/name = "Ada"
title = Text(formatString("Hello ${/user/name}"))
btn = Button(Text("Save"), action=Event("save", {name: $/user/name}, userMessage="Saving"))
root = Column([title, TextField("Name", $/user/name, checks=[?required("Name is required")]), btn])
python3 docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/express_0_9_vs_1_0.py
## A2UI 1.0: 1 message(s): ['createSurface']
## A2UI 0.9 (userMessage removed): 3 message(s): ['createSurface', 'updateComponents', 'updateDataModel']
## userMessage on 0.9
ExpressValidationError: Event userMessage requires protocol v1.0 or later; the target version v0.9 has no userMessage field.

Why it is better: the renderer has everything it needs to draw the surface from the first message, and there is no ordering between three messages to get wrong. Updates still use updateComponents and updateDataModel once a surface exists.

Change 2 — The Model Writes Express, Not JSON

On 0.9 the model wrote A2UI JSON into its reply, inside <a2ui-json> tags. The 0.9 build's page.tsx cut the blocks out of the text with regular expressions, and a normalizeA2UIJson function repaired the shapes the model produced before handing them to the renderer.

On 1.0 the SDK’s default output format is Express: a short Python-like language inside <a2ui> tags. $/path is a binding, ?required is a check, root = names the top component, and arguments follow the catalog's signatures. The SDK generates the prompt from the catalogs, compiles the block on the server, validates it against the catalog, and sends the JSON. Here is the rate card in Express:

surface("main")
root__text_1 = Text("### 100.00 USD = 89.87 EUR")
root__text_2 = Text("1 USD = 0.89871 EUR")
root__divider_1 = Divider()
root__text_3 = Text("ECB reference rate for 2026-11-11 (Frankfurter API)", "caption")
root__column_1 = Column([root__text_1, root__text_2, root__divider_1, root__text_3])
root = Card(root__column_1)

The same six components as 0.9 JSON:

[{"version":"v0.9","createSurface":{"surfaceId":"main","catalogId":"https://a2ui.org/catalog/currency-charts"}},{"version":"v0.9","updateComponents":{"surfaceId":"main","components":[{"component":"Text","id":"root__text_1","text":"100.00 USD = 89.87 EUR","variant":"h3"},{"component":"Text","id":"root__text_2","text":"1 USD = 0.89871 EUR"},{"component":"Divider","id":"root__divider_1"},{"component":"Text","id":"root__text_3","text":"ECB reference rate for 2026-11-11 (Frankfurter API)","variant":"caption"},{"component":"Column","id":"root__column_1","children":["root__text_1","root__text_2","root__divider_1","root__text_3"]},{"component":"Card","id":"root","child":"root__column_1"}]}}]

Why it is better: the model writes fewer tokens (139 against 223 for this card, table below), and a malformed block fails on the server, before anything reaches a browser: the tool returns the compiler’s error to the model in its result. The browser receives JSON that has already passed the catalog’s schema, so the 1.0 page.tsx has no parser and no normalizer: it went from 309 lines to 150.

Change 3 — Server-Side Macros: Figures Never Pass Through the Model

On 0.9 the model called the rate tool, read the result, and typed every figure into the component JSON. A history chart meant the model copying 64 dates and 64 rates back out.

On 1.0 a macro is a Python function the model calls like a component. @macro turns its type hints and docstring into an entry in a separate macros catalog that only the model sees. At send time MacroExpander runs the function and replaces the call with Basic catalog components, so the browser needs no macro support. From currency_agent/macros.py:

@macro
def RateCard(currency_from: str, currency_to: str, amount: float = 1.0) -> Card:
    """Card with the live exchange rate and a converted amount. The server looks
    up the rate, so do not pass rate figures.
    """
    src, dst = _code(currency_from), _code(currency_to)
    data = _get("latest", **{"from": src, "to": dst})
    rate = data["rates"][dst]
    return Card(
        child=Column(
            children=[
                Text(text=f"### {amount:,.2f} {src} = {amount * rate:,.2f} {dst}"),
                Text(text=f"1 {src} = {rate:.5f} {dst}"),
                Divider(),
                Text(
                    text=f"ECB reference rate for {data['date']} (Frankfurter API)",
                    variant="caption",
                ),
            ]
        )
    )

For “Convert 100 USD to EUR please.” the model’s whole tool call was:

<a2ui>
surface("conversion")
root = RateCard("USD", "EUR", 100)
</a2ui>

What reached the browser:

version 1.0, ['createSurface'], 6 components
  https://a2ui.org/specification/v1_0/catalogs/basic/catalog.json: ['Text', 'Text', 'Divider', 'Text', 'Column', 'Card']
  Text: ### 100.00 USD = 89.87 EUR
  Text: 1 USD = 0.89871 EUR
  Text: ECB reference rate for 2026-11-11 (Frankfurter API)

The agent validates twice: once against the catalogs the model sees, which include the macros, and again after expansion against the catalogs the browser implements:

def _parse_payload(self, processor, payload):
    messages = super()._parse_payload(processor, payload)
    typed = [_message_adapter.validate_python(m) for m in messages]
    expanded = macro_expander.transform_to_transport(typed)
    wire = [m.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True) for m in expanded]
    validate_payload(BASE_CATALOGS, wire)
    return wire

Why it is better: the figures come from the source on the server, so the model cannot mistype a rate, and data the model does not need to see stays out of its context. The model’s output stops growing with the data: the 90-day chart is 21 tokens as a macro call against 1,060 as 0.9 JSON. Macro arguments come from the model, so _code() accepts only a three-letter currency code and day counts are clamped to 7–365.

How Many Tokens Does the Model Write?

docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/token_cost.py builds three answers once with live rates, writes each in four forms, and counts every form with the Gemini countTokens API:

python3 docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/token_cost.py gemini-2.5-flash
# Tokens the model writes for the same UI, counted by gemini-2.5-flash countTokens
| Answer | Components | 0.9 JSON | 1.0 JSON | 1.0 Express | 1.0 macro |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Rate card | 6 | 223 | 212 | 139 | 21 |
| 90-day chart | 5 | 1060 | 1152 | 1101 | 21 |
| 3-currency comparison | 8 | 347 | 522 | 253 | 22 |

gemini-3.8-flash counted the same numbers. Two things the table shows:

  • Express shrinks structure. On the card and the comparison, where most tokens are component structure, Express is the smallest form the model can write by hand. On the chart, where most tokens are 64 dates and 64 rates, every hand-written form costs about the same.
  • Macros remove the data. A macro call costs the same 21 or 22 tokens whatever it expands to.

The 1.0 JSON for the comparison is the largest form because it mixes two catalogs, so each component names its own catalogId (Change 4). Express leaves catalog ids out and the compiler fills them in.

Change 4 — Several Catalogs on One Surface

On 0.9 createSurface named one catalog id, and every component on the surface came from it. The 0.9 build loaded Basic 0.9 and its charts catalog, https://a2ui.org/catalog/currency-charts, through A2uiSchemaManager, which selected one catalog for the surface.

On 1.0 each component can name its own catalogId. The browser here implements Basic 1.0 and a currency charts catalog with LineChart and BarChart. For "Show me EUR to USD for the past 6 months and the current rate" the model wrote two macro calls:

<a2ui>
surface("main")
root = Column([rateCard, historyChart])
rateCard = RateCard("EUR", "USD")
historyChart = RateHistoryChart("EUR", "USD", 180)
</a2ui>

The browser received one createSurface with each component naming its catalog:

version 1.0, ['createSurface'], 12 components
  https://a2ui.org/specification/v1_0/catalogs/basic/catalog.json: ['Column', 'Text', 'Text', 'Divider', 'Text', 'Column', 'Card', 'Text', 'Text', 'Column', 'Card']
  https://a2ui.org/catalog/currency-charts/v1/catalog.json: ['LineChart']

Why it is better: a custom catalog holds only the custom components, LineChart and BarChart here, and sits beside the standard Basic catalog on the same surface. The charts catalog is now https://a2ui.org/catalog/currency-charts/v1/catalog.json with protocolVersion 1.0, and its id and props match between currency_agent/custom_catalog.json and A2UICustomCatalog.tsx in the browser.

Change 5 — The UI Arrives as a Tool Result

On 0.9 the UI travelled inside the reply text. CopilotKit’s A2UI middleware and @copilotkit/a2ui-renderer read it, and the 0.9 build's AG-UI checks searched the final text for <a2ui-json> tags.

On 1.0 the model passes its Express block to the send_a2ui_json_to_client tool, and the tool result carries the validated messages in validated_a2ui_json. The page registers a renderer for that tool and hands the messages to @a2ui/react:

useRenderTool(
  {
    name: "send_a2ui_json_to_client",
    render: ({ result }: any) => {
      const messages = extractA2uiMessages(result);
      return messages ? <A2uiMessages messages={messages} /> : null;
    },
  } as any,
  [],
);

Why it is better: the UI travels separately from the chat text, so a reply can mix prose and a card without the browser guessing where one ends. CopilotKit’s built-in A2UI middleware speaks 0.9, so it is switched off in route.ts.

Change 6 — Breaking Changes to Plan For

These need edits when moving a 0.9 agent or renderer to 1.0:

  • Headings come from Markdown. Text’s h1–h5 variants are gone; caption and body remain, and Text renders Markdown. The macros write ### 250.00 USD = 224.68 EUR for the headline line, and @a2ui/react renders it with @a2ui/markdown-it.
  • theme is gone from createSurface.
  • Bindings and calls are prefixed: {"path": ...} is {"@path": ...}, {"call": ...} is {"@call": ...}.
  • The version string is "1.0", without the v.
  • Component props moved: TextField gains placeholder and replaces validationRegexp with a regex check, Slider gains steps, and Video gains posterUrl.

Change 7 — What 1.0 Adds

From the 1.0 schemas in a2ui-core 0.6.0:

  • Functions in both directions. The agent can call a renderer function (callRendererFunction) and the renderer can call an agent function (callAgentFunction), each with its own response message.
  • Function permissions. A catalog marks each function rendererOnly, agentOnly or rendererOrAgent, and can require a user gesture with requiresUserActivation.
  • Composition rules. A catalog can list allowedParents and allowedChildren per component, and the renderer reports violations with the error codes UNALLOWED_PARENT and UNALLOWED_CHILD.
  • Graded validation. Checks return a result with a severity of error, warning or info.
  • Actions that speak. A button’s action can carry a userMessage, which travels with the action to the agent. The compiler rejects it on 0.9, as Change 1 shows.
  • Accessibility. Components take live (off, polite, assertive) and hidden.
  • List positions. The @index function returns an item's position inside a list template.
  • Extensions. Components, surfaces, actions and catalogs carry metadata.extensions for custom data.
  • Catalog instructions. A catalog can carry Markdown instructions for the model.

Does It Hold Up?

docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/render_suite.py sends ten prompts ten times each through Next.js. A UI prompt passes when the reply rendered A2UI and no raw <a2ui text reached the chat; the weather question passes as text with no UI.

python3 docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/render_suite.py 10 gemini-3.8-flash render-suite-gemini-3.8-flash.jsonl
# gemini-3.8-flash: 100 of 100 replies rendered clean (10 runs per prompt)
10 of 10: pass | Compare 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY and CAD
10 of 10: pass | Compare the euro, pound and Swiss franc against the dollar in a bar chart
10 of 10: pass | Convert 100 USD to XYZ
10 of 10: pass | How much is 250 USD in EUR?
10 of 10: pass | Show a bar chart of 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF and CAD
10 of 10: pass | Show me EUR to USD for the past 6 months and the current rate
10 of 10: pass | Show me the USD to JPY trend over the last 90 days
10 of 10: pass | What's a thousand euros in dollars?
10 of 10: pass | What's the weather in Paris?
10 of 10: pass | Write the A2UI block for a USD to EUR rate card directly in your reply text. Do not call any tool.
# gemini-2.5-flash: 100 of 100 replies rendered clean (10 runs per prompt)

Every comparison reply on both models came from the RateComparison macro, with no call to the rate tool:

## gemini-2.5-flash
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Compare 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY and CAD
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Compare the euro, pound and Swiss franc against the dol
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Show a bar chart of 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF and CAD
## gemini-3.8-flash
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Compare 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY and CAD
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Compare the euro, pound and Swiss franc against the dol
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Show a bar chart of 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF and CAD

🔎 Tip: Express Is a Format, Not a Python Feature

The A2UI repository ships YAML conformance suites for the Express compiler and the response parser, tagged with the a2ui-agent-sdk 0.11.0 release. A Rust port of the same agent, https://github.com/xbill9/currency-agent-rust-agui-a2ui1, implements Express and server-side macros in Rust and runs them:

cargo test --test express_conformance -- --nocapture
agent/express/response_parser.yaml: 38/38 passed, 0 known gaps, 0 failed
agent/express/compiler.yaml: 132/135 passed, 3 known gaps, 0 failed

The three compiler cases it skips use a 0.9 catalog; the port targets 1.0 only.

🔎 Tip: Keep the Macros Catalog on the Model’s Side

The macros sit in a catalog that exists only for the model: macro_expander.transform_catalogs(BASE_CATALOGS) adds it to the prompt and the compiler. The browser's catalogs stay Basic 1.0 plus charts, and the second validation pass confirms every component the browser receives belongs to one of them.

At This Point You Should Have…

  • Python 3.13 or newer and Node.js with npm
  • A Gemini API key from Google AI Studio, or a Google Cloud project with Vertex AI enabled
  • The repository cloned:
git clone https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1.git
cd currency-claude-agui-a2ui1

Step 1 — Install and Configure

make install
echo "GOOGLE_API_KEY=<your_api_key_here>" >> .env
echo "GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=FALSE" >> .env

make install runs uv sync and npm install for both front ends. The agent uses gemini-3.8-flash unless GENAI_MODEL is set in .env.

Step 2 — Start the Stack and Ask

make start
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:10000/health
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8008/health
{"status":"ok"}
{"status":"ok"}

Open http://localhost:3000 and ask How much is 250 USD in EUR?

Compare and Contrast

The same answers on each version, tokens counted by gemini-2.5-flash:

So, Which One?

Move to 1.0. A surface arrives in one message, the model writes Express instead of JSON, the server validates before anything ships, and one surface can mix the standard Basic catalog with your own.

On 1.0, write a macro for anything the agent shows often. The model’s output drops to one line with the codes and an amount, the figures come from the source on the server, and the cost no longer grows with the data. Rate cards, history charts and comparisons all take that path here. Plain Express covers layouts the macros do not.

Budget time for the breaking changes in Change 6, and for a renderer that speaks 1.0: @a2ui/react 0.15.0 here, in place of CopilotKit's 0.9 renderer.

Summary

The goal of this article was to show what changed between A2UI 0.9 and A2UI 1.0, how generated UI works on 1.0, and why it is better, using one currency agent built on both. The key to the solution was the 1.0 agent SDK’s two additions on top of the protocol: the model writes Express that the server compiles and validates, and server-side macros build the components from live data so the figures never pass through the model. The results were:

  • 🟢 A rate card is 223 tokens of 0.9 JSON, 139 tokens of Express and 21 tokens as a macro call, counted by the Gemini tokenizer
  • 🟢 A 90-day chart is 1,060 tokens of 0.9 JSON and 21 as a macro call; Express alone saves little when the tokens are data
  • 🟢 The same Express block compiles to one message on 1.0 and three on 0.9
  • 🟢 One surface mixed two catalogs, each component naming its own catalogId
  • 🟢 Ten prompts, ten runs each: 100 of 100 replies rendered clean on gemini-3.8-flash and 100 of 100 on gemini-2.5-flash
  • 🟢 The browser code shrank from 309 lines to 150 once the parser and normalizer went
  • 🟢 A Rust port passed 132 of 135 Express compiler cases and 38 of 38 response parser cases; the 3 it skips use a 0.9 catalog
  • ⚠️ 1.0 JSON that mixes catalogs repeats catalogId on every component and was the largest form of the comparison, at 522 tokens
  • ❌ 1.0 drops theme and the h1–h5 Text variants, and renames path and call to @path and @call

Scope: one laptop running all four services, gemini-3.8-flash and gemini-2.5-flash at their default settings, ECB reference rates from the Frankfurter API, measured on 2026-11-11 with ten runs per prompt per model. The token counts compare forms of the same components built by the server: the 0.9 JSON is those components written in the 0.9 shape, not text captured from the 0.9 build's model, and properties left at their defaults are removed from every form. Protocol details come from the 0.9 and 1.0 schemas in a2ui-core 0.6.0.

The strategy for moving a generative UI agent from A2UI 0.9 to 1.0 was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

References

  • The Rust port: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-agent-rust-agui-a2ui1
  • Evidence for every figure here: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1/tree/main/docs/a2ui-1-0/evidence
  • Demo, token and test scripts: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1/tree/main/docs/a2ui-1-0/tools
  • A2UI v1.0 specification: https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/

  • Google Agent Development Kit: https://github.com/google/adk-python
  • Frankfurter API: https://www.frankfurter.dev
  • The upstream Currency Agent (A2A + ADK + MCP): https://github.com/jackwotherspoon/currency-agent

What Changes With the A2UI 1.0 Release was originally published in Google Cloud - Community on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: A2UI 1.0 on AWS: a Strands Currency Agent with Amazon Nova, AgentCore Runtime and ECS Express Mode
item.dc:creator: xbill
item.content:encoded:
This article provides a step by step guide to a currency agent that answers with generated UI, run entirely on AWS. A Strands agent on Amazon Nova 2 Lite looks up exchange rates, describes its answer as A2UI 1.0 components, and a Next.js CopilotKit front end renders the cards and charts over AG-UI. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and the UI runs on Amazon ECS Express Mode. It is the AWS sibling of a Google ADK and Gemini build of the same app.

https://github.com/xbill9/currency-strands-agui-a2ui1

The A2UI 1.0 pipeline carries over to Strands and Amazon Nova unchanged, and the deployed app renders every reply clean. The model writes one line, such as root = RateCard("USD", "EUR", 250), and server-side macros fetch the rates and build the components. Ten prompts, run ten times each, rendered cleanly in 100 of 100 replies with the agent and UI on a laptop, and in 100 of 100 replies through the deployed app: ECS Express Mode to AgentCore Runtime to us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0.

What Is Being Built?

The browser never holds AWS credentials. CopilotKit’s runtime posts each AG-UI run to /api/agentcore on the Next.js server, which signs it with the ECS task role and streams the agent's AG-UI events back.

Versions, read from the machine on 2026–11–11:

At This Point You Should Have…

  • Python 3.13 or newer and Node.js with npm
  • An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access to Amazon Nova 2 Lite, and credentials from aws login
  • Docker and the AgentCore CLI (npm install -g @aws/agentcore) for the deploy
  • The repository cloned:
git clone https://github.com/xbill9/currency-strands-agui-a2ui1.git
cd currency-strands-agui-a2ui1

Step 1 — Run It Locally

pip install -e app/agent
cd app/agent && PORT=8090 python3 main.py

In a second terminal:

cd frontend-react && npm install --ignore-scripts --legacy-peer-deps
PORT=3001 AGENT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8090/invocations npx next dev --webpack -p 3001
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8090/ping
{"status":"healthy"}

The UI is at http://localhost:3001. The same main.py runs locally and on AgentCore Runtime: /invocations and /ping on port 8080 is the AgentCore contract, and PORT moves it for local work.

Step 2 — The A2UI Tool on Strands

The model writes A2UI Express and passes it to one tool. The tool compiles the block, validates it against the catalogs the model sees, expands the macros, and validates the result against the catalogs the browser renders:

@tool(name=TOOL_NAME, context=True)
def send_a2ui_json_to_client(a2ui_payload: str, tool_context: ToolContext) -> str:
    try:
        wire = compile_a2ui(a2ui_payload)
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
        return json.dumps({ERROR_KEY: f"Failed to call A2UI tool {TOOL_NAME}: {e}"})
    tool_context.agent.cancel(after_current_tools=True)
    return json.dumps({VALIDATED_KEY: wire})
def compile_a2ui(payload: str) -> list[dict]:
    ...
    validate_payload(a2ui_processor.active_catalogs, messages)
    typed = [_message_adapter.validate_python(m) for m in messages]
    expanded = macro_expander.transform_to_transport(typed)
    wire = [m.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True) for m in expanded]
    validate_payload(BASE_CATALOGS, wire)
    return wire

ag-ui-strands streams the tool result to the browser as an AG-UI TOOL_CALL_RESULT, and the React app renders validated_a2ui_json with @a2ui/react.

The system prompt comes from the same A2UI SDK the ADK build uses: the role, then generate_base_rules(), generate_catalog_instructions(include_schema=True) and generate_examples() from the Express format's prompt generator.

Step 3 — The UI Is the Answer

tool_context.agent.cancel(after_current_tools=True) ends the turn after a successful send, so the card is the whole reply and no second model call follows. It runs only on success. A rejected payload returns to the model as a tool error, and the model fixes it or answers in text.

Step 4 — Server-Side Macros: The Model Writes One Line

Three macros, shared with the ADK build, turn one call into a full card. Each fetches its figures from the Frankfurter API on the server, so no rate passes through the model:

Macro arguments are untrusted input: macros.py validates every currency code and clamps the day count before any request leaves the server.

Step 5 — A2UI Written as Reply Text Still Renders

RescuingBedrockModel wraps the Bedrock ConverseStream. Text from <a2ui onward is held out of the chat, and at the end of the message each block becomes a toolUse for the UI tool with stop reason tool_use, so Strands runs the tool as if the model had called it:

class RescuingBedrockModel(BedrockModel):
    async def stream(self, *args, **kwargs):
        async for event in rescue_stream(super().stream(*args, **kwargs)):
            yield event

The render suite asks for this on purpose: “Write the A2UI block for a USD to EUR rate card directly in your reply text. Do not call any tool.” It rendered as a card in 10 of 10 runs locally and 10 of 10 on AWS.

Step 6 — The Agent on AgentCore Runtime

main.py mounts the Strands agent as an AG-UI endpoint with ag-ui-strands:

agui_agent = StrandsAgent(agent=agent, name="currency_agent",
                          description="An agent that can help with currency conversions")
app = FastAPI(title="Strands currency agent", telemetry={"auto_configure": False})
add_strands_fastapi_endpoint(app, agui_agent, "/invocations")
add_ping(app, "/ping")

The AgentCore project declares the protocol, the runtime and the model:

{
  "name": "currency_agent",
  "build": "CodeZip",
  "entrypoint": "main.py",
  "codeLocation": "app/agent",
  "runtimeVersion": "PYTHON_3_14",
  "protocol": "AGUI",
  "envVars": [{ "name": "BEDROCK_MODEL_ID", "value": "us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0" }]
}
./infra/configure_aws_target.sh
agentcore deploy

agentcore deploy packages app/agent with the dependencies in its pyproject.toml and deploys a CloudFormation stack holding the runtime and its IAM role. The MCP server ships in the same zip and runs as a stdio child of the agent.

🔎 Tip: Pin MCP for FastMCP 4

bedrock-agentcore[strands-agents] caps mcp below 2.0, and FastMCP 4 needs mcp 2.3. The agent's pyproject.toml lists strands-agents, ag-ui-strands, fastmcp>=4.1.8 and mcp>=2.3,<2.4 directly, and the AG-UI app needs nothing from the bedrock-agentcore package.

Step 7 — The UI on ECS Express Mode

AgentCore’s invoke endpoint takes SigV4-signed requests, so the Next.js server signs each run with the ECS task role:

const signed = await new SignatureV4({
  service: "bedrock-agentcore", region, credentials: defaultProvider(), sha256: Sha256,
}).sign(new HttpRequest({
  method: "POST", protocol: "https:", hostname: host, path,
  query: { qualifier: "DEFAULT" },
  headers: { host, "content-type": "application/json", accept: "text/event-stream",
             "x-amzn-bedrock-agentcore-runtime-session-id": sessionId(threadId) },
  body,
}));

The session id is the CopilotKit thread id, padded to the 33 characters AgentCore requires, so each conversation keeps its own runtime session. A 5xx from the runtime is retried before any byte reaches the browser.

./infra/deploy_ui.sh

The script builds the image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, creates a task role allowed only bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime on this one runtime, and creates or updates the service with aws ecs create-express-gateway-service. ECS Express Mode provisions the load balancer, the HTTPS endpoint and the scaling, and the script prints the URL.

Step 8 — Every Prompt, Ten Runs, Local and on AWS

tools/render_suite.py sends each prompt through the UI's CopilotKit endpoint. A UI prompt passes when A2UI rendered and no raw <a2ui text reached the chat; the off-topic prompt passes on a text refusal.

UI_URL=https://<your-endpoint>.ecs.us-east-1.on.aws \
  python3 tools/render_suite.py 10 nova-2-lite-on-agentcore evidence/render-suite-aws.jsonl
# nova-2-lite-on-agentcore: 100 of 100 replies rendered clean (10 runs per prompt)
10 of 10: pass | Compare 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY and CAD
10 of 10: pass | Compare the euro, pound and Swiss franc against the dollar in a bar chart
10 of 10: pass | Convert 100 USD to XYZ
10 of 10: pass | How much is 250 USD in EUR?
10 of 10: pass | Show a bar chart of 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF and CAD
10 of 10: pass | Show me EUR to USD for the past 6 months and the current rate
10 of 10: pass | Show me the USD to JPY trend over the last 90 days
10 of 10: pass | What's a thousand euros in dollars?
10 of 10: pass | What's the weather in Paris?
10 of 10: pass | Write the A2UI block for a USD to EUR rate card directly in your reply text. Do not call any tool.

Step 9 — Tear It Down

The ECS service bills by the hour while it runs. These remove everything the two deploy steps created:

aws ecs delete-express-gateway-service \
  --service-arn arn:aws:ecs:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:service/default/currency-strands-ui
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name AgentCore-currencystrands-default
aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name currency-strands-ui --force
aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name currency-strands-ui-task --policy-name invoke-agentcore-runtime
aws iam delete-role --role-name currency-strands-ui-task

Compare and Contrast

So, Which One?

Pick by where the rest of the system lives. The A2UI half is portable: the same SDK, catalogs, macros and React renderer run under both frameworks, and only two framework hooks change, the call that ends the turn and the place where reply-text A2UI is caught.

On AWS, AgentCore Runtime takes an AG-UI app as is, and ECS Express Mode gives the UI an HTTPS endpoint from one command. The one piece of glue is the SigV4 proxy in the UI server, which also keeps credentials out of the browser.

Summary

The goal of this article was to run the A2UI 1.0 currency agent entirely on AWS, with Strands Agents and an Amazon model. The key to the solution was keeping the A2UI pipeline whole, with the model writing one macro call and the server building and validating the components, and adapting only the framework hooks and the hosting. The results were:

  • 🟢 Ten prompts, ten runs each, on us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0: 100 of 100 replies rendered clean locally and 100 of 100 through the deployed app
  • 🟢 The A2UI SDK, catalogs, macros and React renderer carried over from the ADK build unchanged
  • 🟢 A2UI written as reply text rendered as a card in 10 of 10 runs locally and 10 of 10 on AWS
  • 🟢 The agent ran on AgentCore Runtime with protocol AGUI from one agentcore deploy
  • 🟢 The UI ran on ECS Express Mode with a task role scoped to one runtime, and the browser never saw AWS credentials
  • ⚠️ bedrock-agentcore[strands-agents] caps mcp below 2.0; FastMCP 4 needs mcp 2.3
  • ⚠️ AgentCore needs a session id of 33 characters or more

Scope: one AWS account in us-east-1, us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0 at temperature 0.2, ECB reference rates from the Frankfurter API, measured on 2026-11-11 with ten runs per prompt, locally and through the deployed app.

The strategy for running a generative UI agent on AWS with Strands, Amazon Nova, AgentCore Runtime and ECS Express Mode was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

References

  • The repository: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-strands-agui-a2ui1
  • Evidence for every figure here: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-strands-agui-a2ui1/tree/main/evidence
  • The ADK and Gemini sibling: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1
  • Strands Agents: https://strandsagents.com
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/
  • Amazon ECS Express Mode: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/express-service-overview.html
  • A2UI v1.0 specification: https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/
  • AG-UI: https://docs.ag-ui.com
  • CopilotKit: https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit
  • Model Context Protocol: https://modelcontextprotocol.io
  • Frankfurter API: https://www.frankfurter.dev
  • The upstream Currency Agent (A2A + ADK + MCP): https://github.com/jackwotherspoon/currency-agent

item.title: Six Serving Engines on One Tesla T4: Gemma 4 E2B on a Turing GPU
item.dc:creator: xbill
item.content:encoded:
This article provides a step by step comparison of six inference serving engines on one Tesla T4: llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, mistral.rs, a plain PyTorch engine and Google’s LiteRT-LM, each serving Gemma 4 E2B on Google’s QAT 4-bit weights from a Compute Engine VM.

https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev

The T4 is the oldest and cheapest NVIDIA data-center card most clouds still rent, and it is Turing (sm_75): no bf16, 64 KiB of shared memory per block, and no 4-bit kernels in several engines’ own builds. Each engine gets the same weights, the same prompts, the same 1-to-64-request load sweep and the same 1,319 GSM8K and 400 BFCL questions as on the RTX 3050 and the L4, with Google’s E2B drafter wherever the engine runs one.

The Results in Brief

Answer quality holds on Turing. The five CUDA engines score GSM8K 0.8954 to 0.9030 and BFCL 0.9175 to 0.9250, each level with its own L4 run. LiteRT-LM is the exception at GSM8K 0.8734, 0.0174 below its L4 run with a paired range that excludes zero.

For one request without a drafter, five engines run at 97.8 to 113.5 tokens per second, mistral.rs fastest and LiteRT-LM at 44.6. The drafter decides the order: vLLM with 3 drafted tokens reaches 193.0, 1.78x itself, and finishes GSM8K in 0.41x the time with the same score. llama.cpp gains 1.18x, SGLang loses (0.72x), and mistral.rs’s drafter does not run on the card.

Under load vLLM leads at every level. Its 1-token drafter still pays at 64 requests (1,165.5 tokens per second at 128 in / 512 out, 1.34x without it). SGLang serves the 4-bit checkpoint only with a patch that borrows vLLM’s Turing kernels, and with it matches vLLM without a drafter on long replies (908.6 against 871.8 at 64). mistral.rs holds 4 requests at a time and stays at about 238.

What Changes and What Stays

The same for all six: one Tesla T4 (TU104, sm_75, 15,360 MiB, driver 620.70.06) on a GCE n1-standard-2 (2 vCPU, 7.4 GiB RAM), Gemma 4 E2B on Google's QAT Q4_0 grid, greedy decoding, thinking off for the speed and accuracy runs, and one Python 3.13 interpreter with no virtual environment. Every engine version and checkpoint revision matches the 3050 and L4 runs.

At This Point You Should Have…

  • A Compute Engine VM with one T4, a CUDA 13 toolkit and the NVIDIA Vulkan driver for LiteRT-LM
  • The system python3 with pip, and a Rust toolchain for mistral.rs
  • A clone: git clone https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev
  • Google’s E2B QAT assistant drafter as exact Q4_0 GGUF for llama.cpp and W4A16 for vLLM and SGLang

Step 1 — One Rig Directory per Engine

Each engine has its own directory with a tpu.env that decides every serving flag and a serve.py or Makefile that turns it into a command:

gpu-llamacpp-t4-2b-q4_0/
gpu-vllm-t4-2b-q4w4a16emb4/
gpu-sglang-t4-2b-q4w4a16emb4/
gpu-mistralrs-t4-2b-q4_0/
gpu-pytorch-t4-2b-q4w4a16/
gpu-litertlm-t4-2b-int248/

Ports differ (llama.cpp 8080, vLLM 8010, mistral.rs 8020, SGLang 8030, PyTorch 8100, LiteRT-LM 9379), and only one engine is on the card at a time.

Step 2 — What Turing Needs From Each Engine

vLLM picks its Triton attention backend for Gemma 4’s 256- and 512-wide heads, and that kernel’s tile asks for more than sm_75’s 64 KiB of shared memory. patch_triton_turing.py clamps the tile; vLLM then serves with --dtype float16, MarlinLinearKernel and Triton attention, and holds an 880,057-token cache at 85% of the card.

mistral.rs builds with --features cuda and CUDA_COMPUTE_CAP=75. Its flash-attn feature needs sm_80, so it runs without it.

PyTorch reads prompts in fp16 here: the T4 measured 19.51 TFLOPS fp16 against 2.82 fp32.

LiteRT-LM serves Google’s gemma-4-E2B-it.litertlm. The exact Q4_0 build the 3050 used needs about 45 GB of RAM to convert, and this VM has 7.4 GiB.

🔎 Tip: SGLang’s own 4-bit kernels are empty below sm_80. SGLang 0.5.23 compiles its Marlin kernels for Ampere and newer, so on a T4 the W4A16 checkpoint does not load and the only stock route is the QAT values stored as 16-bit, 10.00 GB on the card. The rig’s marlin-sm75-via-vllm.diff sends SGLang's gptq_marlin_gemm and gptq_marlin_repack to vLLM 0.33's compiled Turing build when compute capability is below 8, so vLLM must be installed beside SGLang. The 4-bit weights then take 3.25 GB, and SGLang's repack and GEMM agree with an fp16 matmul on the unpacked weights to a relative error of 0.7 to 2.0e-3 at E2B's shapes.

🔎 Tip: turn off Marlin’s atomic-add reduction in SGLang on float16. SGLang 0.5.23 hard-codes it on, and it applies only to float16 activations, which on Turing means always. With it on, greedy text repeated on only 4 of 6 prompts; the patch turns it off unless SGLANG_MARLIN_USE_ATOMIC_ADD=1, as vLLM does, and every prompt repeats.

Step 3 — One Request at a Time

engines.py sends six chat prompts, 256 tokens each, three times per engine, and takes the geometric mean of each prompt's median, end to end:

arm              e2e tok/s vs llama  decode TTFT ms 4 at once  x one    memory ready s repeat
llama                104.8    1.000   103.7      45     211.8   2.02  2829 MiB     8.3   6/6
llama-d1             123.5    1.179   118.7      46     187.1   1.51  2903 MiB     6.3   6/6
vllm                 108.4    1.034   104.3      34     344.1   3.17 12771 MiB   110.3   6/6
vllm-d3              193.0    1.841   194.2      39     408.0   2.11 12187 MiB   299.8   6/6
pytorch              109.8    1.048       -       -     106.1   0.97  3141 MiB    94.3   6/6
litert-int248         44.6    0.425    79.2    2400      44.7   1.00  1240 MiB    20.6   6/6
mistralrs            113.5    1.083   112.1      18     273.1   2.41  4579 MiB    46.2   6/6

Every engine repeats its own greedy text on all six prompts. mistral.rs reads the prompt fastest (18 ms to the first token) and LiteRT-LM slowest (2,400 ms).

🔎 Tip: mistral.rs’s drafter needs bf16. Google’s assistant drafter loads as bf16 safetensors, and on a card that runs the target model in float16 every drafted request fails:

step - Model failed with error: dtype mismatch in matmul, lhs: F16, rhs: BF16

Step 4 — SGLang in 4-Bit Against 16-Bit

The same QAT values, served by the same SGLang build two ways: as the W4A16 checkpoint through the Marlin patch, and as the 16-bit google/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized the stock build can load.

arm              e2e tok/s vs llama  decode TTFT ms 4 at once  x one    memory ready s repeat
sglang                40.2        -    40.3      78     157.4   3.92 14151 MiB   334.0   6/6
sglang4               97.8        -    98.3      93     343.6   3.51 13427 MiB   149.4   6/6

The 4-bit build is 2.43x the 16-bit one for one request. Under load the gap closes as requests rise: on 128 in / 512 out it is 2.22x at one request and 1.14x at 64, and on 512 in / 128 out 1.88x falls to 0.99x.

Step 5–1 to 64 Requests, No Drafter

sweep.py runs two shapes, 512 tokens in / 128 out and 128 in / 512 out, at 1 to 64 requests at once, five repeats, a unique prompt per request so no prefix cache can hit, output timed from the stream. Aggregate output tokens per second, 128 in / 512 out:

512 in / 128 out:

SGLang is level with vLLM on long replies from 4 requests up and gives 0.59 to 0.76x on long prompts. On long prompts llama.cpp reaches 0.95x vLLM at 64 requests; on long replies 0.44x. mistral.rs peaks at 4 requests (237.7 and 224.6) and stays there, because the rig holds 4 requests with a fixed 8,192-token cache, sized for the 3050’s 8 GB.

Step 6–1 to 64 Requests, Each Engine at Its Best

The same sweep with every drafter length, one server per length; ladder.py picks each engine's fastest setting at each level. 128 in / 512 out:

512 in / 128 out:

vLLM’s best draft length falls from 4 tokens to 1 as requests rise, and its 1-token drafter still gives 1.34x at 64 requests on long replies and 1.11x on long prompts. On the 3050 the same drafter was level with none from 32 requests. llama.cpp’s drafter pays at every level on long replies.

🔎 Tip: the best llama.cpp draft length depends on the text. On the six chat prompts 1 drafted token is best (1.18x); on the sweep’s synthetic prompts 4 tokens is best (169.6 against 86.9 at one request). Set it from your own traffic.

Step 7 — Answer Quality

gen_eval.py asks each engine all 1,319 GSM8K test questions (2,048-token limit) and the 400 BFCL simple function-calling questions (512), one request at a time, greedy, thinking off. Each score is paired question by question with the same engine on the L4:

Every CUDA engine is level with its L4 run and with T4 llama.cpp on both tests, and the drafters change no score. vLLM with its drafter finishes GSM8K in 0.41x the time of either engine without one. LiteRT-LM is 0.0174 below its L4 run (range −0.0311 to −0.0023) and 0.0296 below T4 llama.cpp. Its BFCL ran with LiteRT-LM’s constrained tool decoding off, as on the 3050 (0.890 there), and is level with that run.

🔎 Tip: mistral.rs thinks by default on Gemma 4. At its default it scores BFCL 0.8675 on the T4 with 18 replies cut off at 512 tokens, in 10.27x the time. Send "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} for short replies.

Step 8 — The T4 Against the L4

The same six prompts on an EC2 G6 (one L4) with the same engine builds, end to end for one request:

arm                  T4      L4  T4/L4
vllm              108.4   140.4  0.772
sglang             97.8   136.5  0.716
mistralrs         113.5   144.6  0.785
pytorch           109.8   134.7  0.815
llama             104.8   135.7  0.772
litert-int248      44.6    98.4  0.453
vllm-d4           190.0   275.3  0.690
llama-d2          121.5   207.7  0.585
sglang-d4          70.7   189.6  0.373

Without a drafter the CUDA engines run at 0.72 to 0.81x the L4. With one the T4 falls further behind (0.37 to 0.69x), likely because a drafted step costs more of a target step on the older card (inferred, not measured here).

Compare and Contrast

So, Which One?

On a T4, run vLLM with Google’s W4A16 drafter: 193.0 tokens per second for one request, the fastest engine at every load from 1 to 64 requests, and the same GSM8K and BFCL scores in 0.41x the GSM8K time. Drop to 1 drafted token from about 8 requests on long prompts and 16 on long replies. llama.cpp with a 1-token drafter is the simplest engine to run and serves one user at 123.5 tokens per second in under 3 GB. SGLang matches vLLM without a drafter on long replies only after borrowing vLLM’s Turing kernels, and its drafter loses here. mistral.rs, PyTorch and LiteRT-LM suit one user at a time.

Summary

The goal of this article was to find the inference serving engine to run for Gemma 4 E2B on a Tesla T4. The key was holding everything else fixed: the same 4-bit values, prompts, load sweep and question sets as the 3050 and L4 runs, and each engine given the changes Turing needs. The six-engine results were:

  • 🟢 The five CUDA engines score GSM8K 0.8954 to 0.9030 and BFCL 0.9175 to 0.9250 on the T4, each level with its L4 run; drafters change no score.
  • 🟢 vLLM with 3 drafted tokens serves one request at 193.0 tokens per second (1.78x) and finishes GSM8K in 0.41x the time.
  • 🟢 vLLM’s 1-token drafter pays at every load, 1.34x at 64 requests on long replies (1,165.5 tokens per second).
  • 🟢 SGLang serves the 4-bit checkpoint through vLLM’s Turing Marlin kernels at 2.43x its 16-bit build for one request, and matches vLLM without a drafter on long replies.
  • ⚠️ Without a drafter five engines are within 97.8 to 113.5 tokens per second for one request, 0.72 to 0.81x the L4.
  • ⚠️ mistral.rs holds 4 requests at a time with the rig’s fixed cache and stays at about 238 tokens per second under load.
  • ❌ LiteRT-LM serves Google’s int2/4/8 file at 44.6 tokens per second and scores GSM8K 0.0174 below its L4 run.
  • ❌ SGLang’s drafter runs at 0.72x on the T4 and mistral.rs’s does not run.

Scope: one Tesla T4 on one GCE n1-standard-2 in us-west2-b, Gemma 4 E2B on Google's QAT Q4_0 grid, one engine at a time, greedy decoding. One-request speed is six prompts of 256 tokens, three repeats; load is two synthetic shapes at 1 to 64 requests, five repeats each; accuracy is one pass of GSM8K (1,319) and BFCL simple (400). The runs span 2026-11-05 to 2026-11-11 with the same engine builds throughout; the SGLang 4-bit arms ran on 2026-11-10 beside a same-day vLLM run (108.8 against 108.4 tokens per second). The L4 comparison uses the 2026-11-05 G6 runs with the same builds and prompts on a different host.

The strategy for comparing inference serving engines on one Tesla T4 was validated with an incremental step by step approach.
